claim: Acute glucose starvation induces a dramatic cessation of chromatin movement in budding yeast.
source: Whereas several changes in growth conditions, including growth in different carbon sources or nitrogen starvation, had no obvious effect on chromatin mobility (data not shown), acute glucose starvation induced a dramatic cessation of chromatin movement (Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observations and data shown in Figure 1A comparing chromatin mobility in glucose-containing versus glucose-depleted conditions.

claim: Chromatin mobility is regulated by the presence of glucose.
source: This suggests that chromatin mobility is regulated by the presence of glucose.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental observation that glucose starvation affects chromatin movement.

claim: Glucose starvation leads to an approximately three-fold reduction of the apparent diffusion coefficient for the POA1 locus.
source: We find that the confinement of chromatin upon glucose starvation (Figure 1B and C; Figure 1—figure supplement 2) leads to an approximately three-fold reduction of the apparent diffusion coefficient (K): for instance, KPOA1 decreased from 5.7 x 10–3 µm2/s to 2.3 x 10–3 µm2/s upon starvation (Table 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative measurements of diffusion coefficients presented in Table 1 and Figure 1B and C.

claim: The change in chromatin mobility upon glucose starvation is not caused by a change in the anomaly of the diffusion process.
source: The change in mobility at this time scale was not caused by a change in the anomaly of the diffusion process as the anomalous diffusion exponent (α), which is given by the slope of the curves in the MSD log-log plot, is not affected (see also Table 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of anomalous diffusion exponents shown in Table 1 and MSD plots.

claim: Glucose starvation causes a dramatic reduction in the mobility of cytoplasmic mRNPs.
source: Yet, upon glucose starvation, GFA1 and FBA1 mRNPs also exhibited a dramatic reduction in their mobility (Figure 1E and F; Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing mRNP mobility changes in Figure 1E and F.

claim: Removal of glucose leads to a three- to four-fold decrease in the diffusion coefficient of GFA1 mRNPs.
source: Removal of glucose led to a three- to four-fold decrease in the diffusion coefficient of both GFA1 (KGFA1reduced from 4.2 x 10–2 µm2/s to 1.3 x 10–2 µm2/s) and FBA1 (KFBA1reduced from 5.0 x 10–2 µm2/s to 1.4 x 10-2 µm2/s) mRNPs without affecting the anomalous exponent (α).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative measurements of diffusion coefficients for mRNPs.

claim: Glucose starvation causes a confinement of macromolecules in both the nucleus and the cytoplasm.
source: The decrease in mobility of both chromosomal loci and mRNP particles suggests that glucose starvation causes a confinement of macromolecules in the nucleus as well as the cytoplasm.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that both nuclear chromatin and cytoplasmic mRNPs show reduced mobility upon glucose starvation.

claim: Actin filaments rapidly depolymerize upon starvation.
source: Interestingly, actin filaments were also shown to rapidly depolymerize upon starvation (Uesono et al., 2004; Sagot et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The starvation condition leads to ablation of actin filaments in nearly all cells.
source: Indeed, our starvation condition lead to ablation of actin filaments in nearly all cells (Figure 2A) and a nearly four-fold reduction of microtubule elongation events in G1 cells as visualized by Tub1-GFP (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A quantifying filamentous actin.

claim: Glucose starvation leads to a nearly four-fold reduction of microtubule elongation events in G1 cells.
source: Indeed, our starvation condition lead to ablation of actin filaments in nearly all cells (Figure 2A) and a nearly four-fold reduction of microtubule elongation events in G1 cells as visualized by Tub1-GFP (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Treatment with either nocodazole or latrunculin A reduces chromatin movement, but the effect is insufficient to mimic the confinement of chromatin during starvation.
source: Indeed, treatment with either drug reduced chromatin movement, although the effect was insufficient to mimic the confinement of chromatin during starvation (Figure 2C; Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data comparing drug treatments to starvation conditions shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Concurrent treatments with latrunculin A and nocodazole reduce chromatin mobility in an additive manner.
source: Concurrent treatments with LatA and nocodazole reduced chromatin mobility in an additive manner to substantially reduce chromatin mobility (Figure 2C; Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing combined drug effects in Figure 2C.

claim: The effect of inhibiting the cytoskeleton is most apparent at longer time intervals and may augment the anomalous behavior of chromatin motion.
source: Moreover, log-log MSD plots indicate that the effect of inhibiting the cytoskeleton is most apparent at longer time intervals and may augment the anomalous behavior of chromatin motion (αPOA1-DMSO = 0.56 versus αPOA1-Noc+LatA = 0.48; Figure 2C; Figure 2—figure supplement 1; Table 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of MSD plots and anomalous diffusion exponents shown in Table 1.

claim: Actin and microtubule dynamics independently contribute to the mobility of yeast chromatin.
source: In conclusion, actin and microtubule dynamics independently contribute to the mobility of yeast chromatin.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from experiments showing that both actin and microtubule inhibitors affect chromatin mobility.

claim: mRNP mobility is only moderately affected by perturbation of cytoskeletal dynamics.
source: In contrast to chromatin mobility, mRNP mobility was only moderately affected by perturbation of cytoskeletal dynamics (Figure 2D; Figure 2—figure supplement 1) suggesting that the mobility of the GFA1 and FBA1 mRNPs is largely independent of the cytoskeleton.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D comparing mRNP mobility with and without cytoskeletal inhibitors.

claim: The mobility of GFA1 and FBA1 mRNPs is largely independent of the cytoskeleton.
source: In contrast to chromatin mobility, mRNP mobility was only moderately affected by perturbation of cytoskeletal dynamics (Figure 2D; Figure 2—figure supplement 1) suggesting that the mobility of the GFA1 and FBA1 mRNPs is largely independent of the cytoskeleton.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that cytoskeletal inhibitors have minimal effects on mRNP mobility.

claim: Glucose starvation restricts cytoskeleton-independent mobility as well as the mobility of macromolecules influenced by the cytoskeleton.
source: Overall, our results show that glucose starvation restricts cytoskeleton-independent mobility as well as the mobility of macromolecules influenced by the cytoskeleton.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from experiments showing effects on both chromatin and mRNPs.

claim: Upon glucose starvation, the ATP concentration rapidly decreased by approximately 70%.
source: Upon glucose starvation, the ATP concentration rapidly decreased by ~70%.
evidence: The claim is supported by ATP measurements shown in Figure 3A.

claim: After the initial drop in ATP upon glucose starvation, ATP levels are relatively stable at approximately 30% of the initial concentration.
source: Remarkably, after this initial drop, ATP levels were relatively stable at ~30% of the initial concentration for the remainder of the experiment (Figure 3A).
evidence: The claim is supported by time-course ATP measurements shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The maintenance of reduced ATP levels during glucose starvation requires oxidative phosphorylation.
source: Of note, the maintenance of this reduced ATP level required oxidative phosphorylation as the cellular ATP concentration quickly dropped to nearly undetectable levels when cells deficient in mitochondrial function were starved (cbp2∆; Shaw and Lewin, 1997) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data using cbp2∆ mutant cells shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: When glucose-starved cells are back-diluted into media containing glucose, ATP levels recover to the initial concentration within 30 minutes.
source: In contrast, when cells washed in sugar-free medium were back-diluted into media containing glucose, ATP levels recovered to the initial concentration within 30.
evidence: The claim is supported by ATP recovery experiments shown in Figure 3A.

claim: A ~70% reduction in intracellular ATP levels is insufficient to fully explain the confinement of macromolecular mobility during glucose starvation.
source: We therefore conclude that a ~70% reduction of intracellular ATP, as observed in glucose-depleted cells, is insufficient to fully explain the confinement of macromolecular mobility during glucose starvation.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from experiments showing that azide treatment, which reduces ATP to similar levels as starvation, does not fully replicate the mobility confinement.

claim: The intracellular pH of budding yeast decreases from pH ~7.3 to pH ~6.4 upon glucose deprivation.
source: The intracellular pH (pHi) of budding yeast was reported to decrease from pH ~7.3 to pH ~6.4 in a time frame consistent with the observed confinement of macromolecular mobility upon glucose deprivation (Orij et al., 2009; Young et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies and confirmed by the authors' own measurements.

claim: Glucose starvation causes a reduction in intracellular pH from ~7.4 to ~6.4.
source: Using the pH-sensitive GFP analog, pHluorin, as a pHi biosensor (Miesenböck et al., 1998), we confirmed in our experimental conditions that glucose starvation causes a reduction in pHi from ~7.4 to ~6.4 (Figure 4A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental measurements using pHluorin shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Exposing cells to increasing concentrations of potassium sorbate induces macromolecular confinement.
source: Remarkably, exposing cells to increasing concentrations of K+Sorbate induced macromolecular confinement, and both chromatin and mRNP mobility could be titrated with decreasing pHi (Figure 4C–F; Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing dose-dependent effects of K+Sorbate on macromolecular mobility in Figures 4C-F.

claim: Treatment with 8 mM potassium sorbate is necessary to fully recapitulate the starvation-induced confinement of both chromatin and mRNPs.
source: Importantly, however, treatment with the highest concentration of K+Sorbate (8 mM) was necessary to fully recapitulate the starvation-induced confinement of both chromatin and mRNPs (Figure 4C–F).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data comparing different K+Sorbate concentrations shown in Figures 4C-F.

claim: Treatment with 8 mM potassium sorbate lowers intracellular pH to 5.9, which is below the physiologically observed pH of 6.4 in glucose-starved cells.
source: Under this condition, pHi dropped to 5.9, which is below the physiologically observed pHi of 6.4 in glucose-starved cells (Figure 4A).
evidence: The claim is supported by pH measurements shown in Figure 4A.

claim: When intracellular pH is lowered to 6.4 by addition of 2 mM potassium sorbate, the movement of both chromatin and mRNPs is only moderately reduced.
source: When pHi was lowered to 6.4 (by the addition of 2 mM K+Sorbate), the movement of both chromatin and mRNPs was only moderately reduced (Figure 4C–F).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 4C-F.

claim: Starvation in glucose-free media adjusted to pH 7.4 fails to inhibit the confinement of chromatin and mRNPs upon glucose starvation.
source: Furthermore, starvation in (–) glucose media adjusted to pH 7.4, which prevents a drop in intracellular pH (Dechant et al., 2010), failed to inhibit the confinement of chromatin and mRNPs upon glucose starvation (Figure 4G and H).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 4G and H and a citation to Dechant et al., 2010.

claim: The starvation-induced reduction of intracellular pH is neither sufficient nor necessary to fully explain the observed confinement of macromolecular mobility.
source: Thus, the starvation-induced reduction of pHi is neither sufficient nor necessary and cannot fully explain the observed confinement of macromolecular mobility.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from experiments showing that pH changes alone do not account for the mobility confinement.

claim: Nuclear volume decreases upon glucose withdrawal.
source: In the course of our experiments, we found that the nuclear volume decreased upon glucose withdrawal (Figure 5A).
evidence: The claim is supported by nuclear volume measurements shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Nuclear volume and cellular volume are generally tightly linked.
source: Since nuclear volume and cellular volume are generally tightly linked (Neumann and Nurse, 2007; Jorgenesen et al., 2002), we utilized a Coulter Counter to examine whether cell size changes upon glucose starvation.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The median cell volume decreases from 101.6 fL to 86.1 fL upon glucose starvation, corresponding to a volume reduction of approximately 15%.
source: Indeed, the median cell volume decreased from 101.6 fL (σ = 54.6) in glucose to 86.1 fL (σ = 45.6) in starved cells, corresponding to a volume reduction of ~15% (Figure 5B).
evidence: The claim is supported by cell volume measurements shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The yeast vacuole swells in size under glucose starvation conditions.
source: In addition, we observed that the yeast vacuole, an organelle involved in various processes including protein degradation and metabolite storage, swelled in size under glucose starvation conditions (Figure 5C).
evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy observations shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The vacuole-to-cell volume ratio increases from 0.25 ± 0.02 in non-starved cells to 0.40 ± 0.01 in starved cells.
source: In non-starved cells, the vacuole-to-cell volume ratio was 0.25 ± 0.02, whereas for starved cells this ratio increased to 0.40 ± 0.01 (mean ± standard error for three independent experiments) (Figure 5D).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative measurements shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Vacuolar volume expansion together with the decrease in total cell and nuclear volume reduces the cytoplasmic space available for diffusing molecules by approximately 30% upon glucose starvation.
source: In combination, this vacuolar volume expansion together with the decrease in total cell and nuclear volume, reduces the cytoplasmic space that is available for diffusing molecules upon glucose starvation by ~30% ('Materials and methods').
evidence: The claim is based on calculations using measured volume changes.

claim: Lowering intracellular pH by addition of potassium sorbate induces an increasing reduction in cell volume.
source: Remarkably, lowering pHi by the addition of K+Sorbate also induced an increasing reduction in cell volume.
evidence: The claim is supported by cell volume measurements after K+Sorbate treatment shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Addition of 8 mM potassium sorbate reduces the median cell volume to 87.1 fL, a level virtually identical to that of glucose-starved cells.
source: Strikingly, addition of 8 mM K+Sorbate, which led to the same mobility decrease as glucose starvation, reduced the median cell volume to 87.1 fL (σ = 46.3), a level virtually identical to that of glucose-starved cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A and Figure 5B).
evidence: The claim is supported by cell volume measurements comparing K+Sorbate treatment to glucose starvation.

claim: Intracellular acidification is not required for the decrease in cell volume upon starvation.
source: Although intracellular acidification led to a decrease in cell volume, it was not required for this decrease since starvation in (–) glucose media adjusted to pH 7.4, preventing an intracellular pH drop (Dechant et al., 2010), also reduced the cell volume (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by cell volume measurements under pH-controlled conditions shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Addition of NaCl has little effect on intracellular pH or cellular ATP levels.
source: Notably, addition of NaCl had little effect on pHi or cellular ATP levels, allowing us to uncouple the effects of cell volume from these factors (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by measurements shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: Both chromatin and mRNP mobility are progressively confined by increasing the magnitude of osmotic shock.
source: As shown in Figure 5E and F and Figure 5—figure supplement 2C and D, both chromatin and mRNP mobility were progressively confined by increasing the magnitude of osmotic shock, consistent with recent results demonstrating that osmotic shock affects intracellular diffusion (Babazadeh et al., 2013; Miermont et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 5E and F and citations to previous studies.

claim: A reduction of cell volume is sufficient to explain the starvation-induced confinement of macromolecular mobility.
source: Therefore, a reduction of cell volume is sufficient to explain the starvation-induced confinement of macromolecular mobility.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from experiments showing that osmotic shock, which reduces cell volume, can replicate the mobility confinement.

claim: Acute glucose starvation does not induce a decrease in cell mass.
source: Thus, acute glucose starvation does not induce a decrease in cell mass despite a significant reduction in the accessible cellular volume.
evidence: The claim is supported by lyophilization mass measurements shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The dry mass of non-starved yeast cells is 11.5 ± 0.5 pg/cell.
source: We saw no significant difference between the non-starved and starved samples (11.5 ± 0.5 pg/cell and 11.9 ± 0.4 pg/cell, respectively; mean ± standard deviation for three independent experiments).
evidence: The claim is supported by mass measurements shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The dry mass of glucose-starved yeast cells is 11.9 ± 0.4 pg/cell.
source: We saw no significant difference between the non-starved and starved samples (11.5 ± 0.5 pg/cell and 11.9 ± 0.4 pg/cell, respectively; mean ± standard deviation for three independent experiments).
evidence: The claim is supported by mass measurements shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Yeast cells grown continuously in raffinose show a 23% reduction in cell mass compared to cells grown on glucose.
source: Importantly, yeast cells grown continuously in raffinose, which are known to be smaller than cells grown on glucose (Tyson et al., 1979) and thus served as a positive control, showed a 23% reduction in cell mass (8.9 pg/cell) compared to cells grown in glucose.
evidence: The claim is supported by mass measurements shown in Figure 6A and a citation to Tyson et al., 1979.

claim: The increase in mass density upon glucose starvation suggests that the intracellular environment experiences increased molecular crowding conditions.
source: This increase in mass density suggests that the intracellular environment experiences increased molecular crowding conditions, which may lead to broad changes in the material properties of the cell.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that cell volume decreases without a corresponding decrease in mass.

claim: Glucose starvation induces a change in the mechanical properties of budding yeast cells, increasing their mean stiffness from 18 to 22 nN·µm–1.
source: Force-response curves were recorded while compressing single cells and analysis showed that glucose starvation induced a change in the cells' mechanical properties increasing their mean stiffness from 18 to 22 nN·µm–1 as well as increasing the cell-to-cell variability in stiffness (Figure 6B).
evidence: The claim is supported by AFM measurements shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Glucose starvation increases cell-to-cell variability in stiffness.
source: Force-response curves were recorded while compressing single cells and analysis showed that glucose starvation induced a change in the cells' mechanical properties increasing their mean stiffness from 18 to 22 nN·µm–1 as well as increasing the cell-to-cell variability in stiffness (Figure 6B).
evidence: The claim is supported by AFM measurements shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Starved yeast cells are smaller than non-starved control cells.
source: Consistent with the cell size measurements described above (Figure 5B), these AFM experiments also suggest that starved yeast cells are smaller than the corresponding control cells and that there appears to be a negative correlation between cell size and stiffness (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by AFM measurements and cell size measurements shown in Figure 5B and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: There is a negative correlation between cell size and stiffness in yeast.
source: Consistent with the cell size measurements described above (Figure 5B), these AFM experiments also suggest that starved yeast cells are smaller than the corresponding control cells and that there appears to be a negative correlation between cell size and stiffness (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Starved shmooed spheroplasts remain predominantly in an elongated form, approximately four-fold less spherical than non-starved spheroplasts.
source: Intriguingly, starved shmooed spheroplasts remained predominantly in an elongated form (~four-fold less spherical spheroplasts in starved versus non-starved conditions) (Figure 6C, Video 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy observations shown in Figure 6C and Video 2.

claim: The resistance of starved shmooed spheroplasts to internal turgor pressure suggests that the starved yeast cytoplasm is significantly more rigid than that of non-starved yeast.
source: This resistance to the internal turgor pressure suggests that the starved yeast cytoplasm is significantly more rigid than that of non-starved yeast, consistent with our AFM measurements.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that starved spheroplasts maintain their shape.

claim: The stiffening of the yeast cytoplasm upon starvation is reversible.
source: Furthermore, this stiffening is reversible as re-addition of glucose to the starved spheroplasts returned them to a spherical form (Video 3), suggesting that sensory feedback pathways may exist to actively regulate this stiffening mechanism.
evidence: The claim is supported by observations shown in Video 3.

claim: Sensory feedback pathways may exist to actively regulate the stiffening mechanism in yeast.
source: Furthermore, this stiffening is reversible as re-addition of glucose to the starved spheroplasts returned them to a spherical form (Video 3), suggesting that sensory feedback pathways may exist to actively regulate this stiffening mechanism.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observation that the stiffening is reversible.

claim: Budding yeast cells undergo dramatic biophysical changes upon acute glucose starvation affecting their viscoelastic properties in addition to their intracellular macromolecular diffusion.
source: Taken together our results demonstrate that budding yeast cells undergo dramatic biophysical changes upon acute glucose starvation affecting their viscoelastic properties in addition to their intracellular macromolecular diffusion.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from multiple experiments showing changes in both diffusion and mechanical properties.

claim: Glucose-starved fission yeast spheroplasts maintain their rod-shape, demonstrating that glucose-withdrawal leads to a stiffening of the cytoplasm.
source: Conversely, glucose-starved cells maintain their rod-shape, reminiscent of the shmooed budding yeast cells, again demonstrating that glucose-withdrawal leads to a remarkable stiffening of the cytoplasm (Figure 6D, Video 5).
evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy observations shown in Figure 6D and Video 5.

claim: The stiffening of fission yeast cytoplasm upon glucose starvation is reversible.
source: As for budding yeast, the stiffening is also reversible as addition of glucose to starved S. pombe spheroplasts returns them to a spherical shape (Video 6).
evidence: The claim is supported by observations shown in Video 6.

claim: Budding and fission yeast separated evolutionarily several hundred million years ago and are as different from each other as either is from metazoans.
source: Budding and fission yeast separated evolutionarily several hundred million years ago, and they are as different from each other as either is from metazoans (Sipiczki, 2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Sipiczki, 2000.

claim: The bacterial cytoplasm has glass-like properties and can undergo liquid-like to solid-like transitions upon starvation or treatment with 2,4-Dinitrophenol (DNP).
source: It was recently reported that the bacterial cytoplasm has glass-like properties and can undergo liquid-like to solid-like transitions upon starvation or treatment with 2,4-Dinitrophenol (DNP), an uncoupler of oxidative phosphorylation (Parry et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Parry et al., 2014.

claim: Starvation or DNP treatment in bacteria results in confinement of macromolecules and disproportionally affects large particles above approximately 30 nm.
source: This condition results in confinement of macromolecules and disproportionally affects large particles above ~30 nm (Parry et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Parry et al., 2014.

claim: A 30 min treatment of E. coli with 2 mM DNP causes a significant reduction in the volume of E. coli, inducing an approximately 9.5% modal volume contraction.
source: Strikingly, a 30 min treatment of E.coli with 2 mM DNP caused a significant reduction in the volume of E.coli, inducing a ~9.5% modal volume contraction (SD = ± 4.1%) (Figure 6E).
evidence: The claim is supported by cell volume measurements shown in Figure 6E.

claim: The liquid-to-solid like phase transition of the bacterial cytoplasm may be triggered by cellular volume loss.
source: Nevertheless, this result suggests that the reported liquid-to-solid like phase transition of the bacterial cytoplasm may also be triggered by cellular volume loss and suggests that the starvation-induced reduction of cell size could be a deeply conserved starvation response.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observation that DNP treatment reduces bacterial cell volume.

claim: The starvation-induced reduction of cell size could be a deeply conserved starvation response.
source: Nevertheless, this result suggests that the reported liquid-to-solid like phase transition of the bacterial cytoplasm may also be triggered by cellular volume loss and suggests that the starvation-induced reduction of cell size could be a deeply conserved starvation response.
evidence: This is speculation based on observations in both bacteria and yeast.

claim: The dramatic macromolecular confinement observed upon starvation of budding yeast cannot be explained by a reduction of intracellular ATP.
source: Our results identify a novel cellular response that severely alters the biophysical properties of cells and restricts intracellular diffusion in response to glucose starvation. The dramatic macromolecular confinement observed upon starvation of budding yeast cannot be explained by a reduction of intracellular ATP (Figure 3), by a drop in pH (Figure 4) or inhibition of global metabolism, as respiration persists upon glucose depletion (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from experiments showing that ATP reduction alone does not account for the mobility confinement.

claim: The dramatic macromolecular confinement observed upon starvation of budding yeast cannot be explained by a drop in pH.
source: Our results identify a novel cellular response that severely alters the biophysical properties of cells and restricts intracellular diffusion in response to glucose starvation. The dramatic macromolecular confinement observed upon starvation of budding yeast cannot be explained by a reduction of intracellular ATP (Figure 3), by a drop in pH (Figure 4) or inhibition of global metabolism, as respiration persists upon glucose depletion (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from experiments showing that pH changes alone do not account for the mobility confinement.

claim: Respiration persists upon glucose depletion in budding yeast.
source: Our results identify a novel cellular response that severely alters the biophysical properties of cells and restricts intracellular diffusion in response to glucose starvation. The dramatic macromolecular confinement observed upon starvation of budding yeast cannot be explained by a reduction of intracellular ATP (Figure 3), by a drop in pH (Figure 4) or inhibition of global metabolism, as respiration persists upon glucose depletion (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by ATP measurements showing that ATP levels are maintained at ~30% through oxidative phosphorylation.

claim: Increased macromolecular crowding induced by an acute volume loss fundamentally alters the mechanical properties of cells leading to macromolecular confinement.
source: Instead, we propose that increased macromolecular crowding induced by an acute volume loss fundamentally alters the mechanically properties of cells leading to macromolecular confinement.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on experimental observations of volume loss and increased stiffness.

claim: Both eukaryotic and prokaryotic cells regulate the level of crowding in order to control intracellular diffusion and macromolecular interactions.
source: Our results further suggest that both eukaryotic and prokaryotic cells regulate the level of crowding in order to control intracellular diffusion and macromolecular interactions.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from observations in both yeast and bacteria.

claim: Metazoan cells rapidly swell during cell division, which might aid with the mitotic separation of large chromosomes.
source: In this context, it is intriguing that metazoan cells also seem to regulate their cellular volume as it was recently reported that tissue culture cells rapidly swell during cell division, which might aid with the mitotic separation of large chromosomes (Zlotek-Zlotkiewicz et al., 2015; Son et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Zlotek-Zlotkiewicz et al., 2015 and Son et al., 2015.

claim: Upon acute glucose starvation, budding yeast cells undergo a notable cytosolic acidification lowering their intracellular pH to approximately 6.4.
source: Upon acute glucose starvation, budding yeast cells undergo a notable cytosolic acidification lowering their intracellular pH to ~6.4, presumably by the rapid inhibition of the major plasma membrane proton pump Pma1 (Figure 4; Orij et al., 2009; Young et al., 2010; Dechant et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by pH measurements and citations to previous studies.

claim: The cytosolic acidification upon glucose starvation is presumably caused by the rapid inhibition of the major plasma membrane proton pump Pma1.
source: Upon acute glucose starvation, budding yeast cells undergo a notable cytosolic acidification lowering their intracellular pH to ~6.4, presumably by the rapid inhibition of the major plasma membrane proton pump Pma1 (Figure 4; Orij et al., 2009; Young et al., 2010; Dechant et al., 2010).
evidence: This is an inference based on citations to previous studies.

claim: pH drop alone is neither necessary nor sufficient to recapitulate the macromolecular confinement upon glucose starvation.
source: Whereas this acidification might contribute to macromolecular confinement and enhance changes of biophysical properties within cells (Fels et al., 2009), pH drop alone is neither necessary nor sufficient to recapitulate the macromolecular confinement, and the volume loss observed in glucose starved cells can occur in the absence of acidification (Figure 4 and Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from experiments manipulating pH independently of glucose starvation.

claim: The volume loss observed in glucose starved cells can occur in the absence of acidification.
source: Whereas this acidification might contribute to macromolecular confinement and enhance changes of biophysical properties within cells (Fels et al., 2009), pH drop alone is neither necessary nor sufficient to recapitulate the macromolecular confinement, and the volume loss observed in glucose starved cells can occur in the absence of acidification (Figure 4 and Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experiments showing volume loss in pH-controlled conditions.

claim: Inhibition of cellular metabolism by 2-deoxyglucose and antimycin provokes an enhanced drop of intracellular pH to 5.5.
source: Interestingly, inhibition of cellular metabolism by 2-deoxyglucose and antimycin also provokes an enhanced drop of intracellular pHto 5.5, which in turn triggers macromolecular confinement and leads to profound changes in the mechanical properties of the cell consistent with a sol to gel-like transition of the cytoplasm (Munder et al., personal communication).
evidence: The claim is supported by a personal communication citation.

claim: Inhibition of cellular metabolism by 2-deoxyglucose and antimycin triggers macromolecular confinement and leads to profound changes in the mechanical properties of the cell consistent with a sol to gel-like transition of the cytoplasm.
source: Interestingly, inhibition of cellular metabolism by 2-deoxyglucose and antimycin also provokes an enhanced drop of intracellular pHto 5.5, which in turn triggers macromolecular confinement and leads to profound changes in the mechanical properties of the cell consistent with a sol to gel-like transition of the cytoplasm (Munder et al., personal communication).
evidence: The claim is supported by a personal communication citation.

claim: The movement of yeast chromatin is strongly influenced by the joint dynamics of both actin and microtubules.
source: Our data also support a mechanism of chromatin mobility in which the movement of yeast chromatin is strongly influenced by the joint dynamics of both actin and microtubules.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from experiments showing that both actin and microtubule inhibitors affect chromatin mobility.

claim: Microtubules interact with spindle pole bodies and centromeres throughout the cell cycle.
source: Precedence for such a mechanism is evidenced by previous work describing similar microtubule-dependent motion and reported interactions between microtubules, spindle pole bodies, and centromeres throughout the cell cycle (Heun et al., 2001; Tanaka and Tanaka, 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Heun et al., 2001 and Tanaka and Tanaka, 2009.

claim: The actin cytoskeleton propels the movement of meiotic chromosomes.
source: Moreover, the actin cytoskeleton is known to propel the movement of meiotic chromosomes and to influence the diffusion of other large macromolecules, suggesting a central function throughout the life cycle of yeast (Koszul et al., 2008; Brangwynne et al., 2009a; Zhou et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Koszul et al., 2008; Brangwynne et al., 2009a; Zhou et al., 2011.

claim: The long-range directional movement of chromosomal loci is dependent on the actin cytoskeleton.
source: The long-range directional movement of chromosomal loci is also reported to be dependent on the actin cytoskeleton (Chuang et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Chuang et al., 2006.

claim: Cytoskeletal inhibitors appear to more strongly affect the mobility of chromatin at longer timescales and have minor effects at shorter ones.
source: This is consistent with our data, as the cytoskeletal inhibitors latrunculin-A and nocodozale appeared to more strongly affect the mobility of chromatin at longer timescales and have minor effects at shorter ones (Figure 2; Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of MSD plots at different timescales shown in Figure 2.

claim: Actin filaments exist in the nucleus.
source: Finally, recent work detailing the existence of actin filaments in the nucleus substantiates the possibility of a network of nuclear actin (Baarlink et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Baarlink et al., 2013.

claim: Treatment with sodium azide had only minor effects on the mobility of chromosomes in one study.
source: Paradoxically, previous experiments exploring the ATP dependence of chromatin mobility reached opposing conclusions in that treatment with sodium azide had only minor effects on the mobility of chromosomes in one study (Marshall et al., 1997) but drastically reduced their mobility in another (Heun et al., 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Marshall et al., 1997.

claim: Treatment with sodium azide drastically reduced chromatin mobility in another study.
source: Paradoxically, previous experiments exploring the ATP dependence of chromatin mobility reached opposing conclusions in that treatment with sodium azide had only minor effects on the mobility of chromosomes in one study (Marshall et al., 1997) but drastically reduced their mobility in another (Heun et al., 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Heun et al., 2001.

claim: Distinct azide treatment protocols reduce intracellular pH to dramatically different extents.
source: Importantly, however, we also observed that azide treatment lowered pHi and that the distinct treatments reduced intracellular pH to dramatically different extents (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by pH measurements shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: A pleiotropic effect of azide treatment on intracellular pH might be sufficient to reconcile the observed differences in the confinement of macromolecules between different studies.
source: Thus, a pleiotropic effect of azide treatment on pHi might be sufficient to reconcile the observed differences in the confinement of macromolecules.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observation that different azide treatments affect pH differently.

claim: Changes in ATP and intracellular pH do not have additive effects on macromolecular mobility.
source: This indicates that changes in ATP and pHi do not have additive effects and are neither alone nor in combination sufficient to explain the effects on macromolecular mobility that we observe in glucose starvation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from experiments showing that azide treatment, which affects both ATP and pH, does not fully replicate starvation effects.

claim: Both chromatin and mRNPs display anomalous subdiffusion at the timescales investigated.
source: As expected (Luby-Phelps, 2000), our single particle-tracking experiments show that both chromatin and mRNPs display anomalous subdiffusion at the timescales that we investigated.
evidence: The claim is supported by MSD analysis and a citation to Luby-Phelps, 2000.

claim: Glucose starvation dramatically decreases the diffusivity of tracked objects but does not change the anomaly of the diffusion.
source: Interestingly, while glucose starvation dramatically decreases the diffusivity of the tracked objects, it does not change the anomaly of the diffusion.
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of diffusion coefficients and anomalous exponents shown in Table 1.

claim: Glucose deprivation induces a dramatic increase of the 'microscopic' viscosity without affecting the higher order cellular structures that impede macromolecule motion.
source: The fact that glucose deprivation affects diffusivity but not anomaly suggests that starvation induces a dramatic increase of the 'microscopic' viscosity without affecting the higher order cellular structures that impede macromolecule motion (Huet et al., 2014).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that diffusivity changes but anomaly does not, with support from a citation to Huet et al., 2014.

claim: The change of microscopic viscosity upon glucose starvation is probably the consequence of an increase in crowding upon cell size contraction.
source: Based on our results and according to the classical molecular crowding theory (Zimmerman and Minton, 1993) this change of microscopic viscosity is probably the consequence of an increase in crowding upon cell size contraction.
evidence: This is an inference based on molecular crowding theory and experimental observations, with a citation to Zimmerman and Minton, 1993.

claim: The modulation of intracellular diffusion represents a mechanism to globally regulate the biochemistry of cells.
source: Notably, this modulation of intracellular diffusion represents a mechanism to globally regulate the biochemistry of cells.
evidence: This is speculation about the functional significance of the observed phenomenon.

claim: Glucose starvation represents a dormant state which might hold cells in stasis until provisions in the environment improve.
source: As described for bacteria (Parry et al., 2014), we envision glucose starvation as a dormant state which might hold cells in stasis until provisions in the environment improve.
evidence: This is speculation about the biological function of the starvation response, with a citation to Parry et al., 2014.

claim: Cells functionally regulate intracellular diffusion in order to establish a cellular organization that is restrictive to some molecular interactions while simultaneously permissive to essential biochemistry.
source: Consequently, we propose that cells functionally regulate intracellular diffusion in order to establish a cellular organization that is restrictive to some molecular interactions, perhaps thereby conserving energy, while simultaneously permissive to essential biochemistry.
evidence: This is a proposed model for the functional significance of the observed phenomenon.

claim: The conservation of cell contraction between prokaryotes and eukaryotes strongly suggests a vital function during starvation.
source: The conservation of cell contraction between prokaryotes and eukaryotes strongly suggests a vital function during starvation.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from observations in both bacteria and yeast.

claim: Pma1p is required for regulation of intracellular pH and uses upwards of 20% of cellular ATP.
source: For example, Pma1p, required for regulation of intracellular pH and thought to use upwards of 20% of cellular ATP, is immediately inhibited upon glucose starvation (Bracey et al., 1998).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Bracey et al., 1998.

claim: Pma1p is immediately inhibited upon glucose starvation.
source: For example, Pma1p, required for regulation of intracellular pH and thought to use upwards of 20% of cellular ATP, is immediately inhibited upon glucose starvation (Bracey et al., 1998).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Bracey et al., 1998.

claim: Ribosomes disengage from mRNA upon glucose starvation, resulting in a global collapse of polysome profiles.
source: Ribosomes also disengage from mRNA, resulting in a global collapse of polysome profiles (Ashe et al., 2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Ashe et al., 2000.

claim: Treatment with latrunculin A rapidly increases intracellular ATP concentrations.
source: Additionally, we found that depolymerization of the actin cytoskeleton may function, in part, to conserve ATP, as treatment with latrunculin A rapidly increases intracellular ATP concentrations (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by ATP measurements shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: Depolymerization of the actin cytoskeleton may function, in part, to conserve ATP.
source: Additionally, we found that depolymerization of the actin cytoskeleton may function, in part, to conserve ATP, as treatment with latrunculin A rapidly increases intracellular ATP concentrations (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that latrunculin A treatment increases ATP levels.

claim: Osmotic shock promptly inhibits translation initiation.
source: Because osmotic shock promptly inhibits translation initiation and depolymerizes the actin cytoskeleton, it is conceivable that the starvation-induced cytoskeletal breakdown and collapse of polysome profiles, as well as other starvation-associated phenotypes, could be partly driven by molecular crowding (Chowdhury et al., 1992; Ueseono et al., 2004; Ashe et al., 2000; Uesono and Toh-EA, 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Chowdhury et al., 1992; Ueseono et al., 2004; Ashe et al., 2000; Uesono and Toh-EA, 2002.

claim: Osmotic shock depolymerizes the actin cytoskeleton.
source: Because osmotic shock promptly inhibits translation initiation and depolymerizes the actin cytoskeleton, it is conceivable that the starvation-induced cytoskeletal breakdown and collapse of polysome profiles, as well as other starvation-associated phenotypes, could be partly driven by molecular crowding (Chowdhury et al., 1992; Ueseono et al., 2004; Ashe et al., 2000; Uesono and Toh-EA, 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Chowdhury et al., 1992; Ueseono et al., 2004; Ashe et al., 2000; Uesono and Toh-EA, 2002.

claim: The starvation-induced cytoskeletal breakdown and collapse of polysome profiles could be partly driven by molecular crowding.
source: Because osmotic shock promptly inhibits translation initiation and depolymerizes the actin cytoskeleton, it is conceivable that the starvation-induced cytoskeletal breakdown and collapse of polysome profiles, as well as other starvation-associated phenotypes, could be partly driven by molecular crowding (Chowdhury et al., 1992; Ueseono et al., 2004; Ashe et al., 2000; Uesono and Toh-EA, 2002).
evidence: This is speculation based on the observation that osmotic shock has similar effects to starvation.

claim: The confinement of intracellular diffusion through molecular crowding may prove vital for economical biochemistry and represent a very upstream event upon carbon starvation.
source: Therefore, the confinement of intracellular diffusion through molecular crowding may prove vital for economical biochemistry and represent a very upstream event upon carbon starvation.
evidence: This is speculation about the functional significance and timing of the observed phenomenon.

claim: Molecular crowding-enhanced aggregation and confined macromolecular mobility may promote sustained interactions between complexes during starvation.
source: On the other hand, molecular crowding-enhanced aggregation and confined macromolecular mobility may promote sustained interactions between complexes during starvation.
evidence: This is speculation about potential functional consequences of molecular crowding.

claim: Starvation induces the formation of compartmentalized biochemistry and potential pockets of liquid-liquid unmixing.
source: In agreement with this hypothesis, starvation is known to induce the formation of compartmentalized biochemistry and potential pockets of liquid-liquid unmixing (Narayanaswamy et al., 2009; Brangwynne et al., 2009b).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Narayanaswamy et al., 2009 and Brangwynne et al., 2009b.

claim: P-bodies form in the absence of glucose and potentially aggregate through unstructured regions of the component proteins.
source: For example, P-bodies, macromolecular complexes composed of mRNPs and mRNA decay machinery, form in the absence of glucose and potentially aggregate through unstructured regions of the component proteins (Ramachandran et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Ramachandran et al., 2011.

claim: Stationary phase induces the formation of foci and filaments for large numbers of proteins.
source: Moreover, stationary phase induces the formation of foci and filaments for large numbers of proteins (Narayanaswamy et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Narayanaswamy et al., 2009.

claim: Protein aggregation in stationary phase was hypothesized to enhance interactions between members of the same pathway and promote more efficient biochemistry.
source: This aggregation was hypothesized to enhance interactions between members of the same pathway and promote more efficient biochemistry (Narayanaswamy et al., 2009) but was more recently also shown to cause enzymatic inactivation in some instances (Petrovska et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Narayanaswamy et al., 2009.

claim: Protein aggregation in stationary phase was shown to cause enzymatic inactivation in some instances.
source: This aggregation was hypothesized to enhance interactions between members of the same pathway and promote more efficient biochemistry (Narayanaswamy et al., 2009) but was more recently also shown to cause enzymatic inactivation in some instances (Petrovska et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Petrovska et al., 2014.

claim: Prolonged starvation and confinement of macromolecular mobility may pose unique challenges to cells, as complexes with elongated stretches of unstructured regions may prove more prone to extensive aggregation.
source: As a consequence, prolonged starvation and confinement of macromolecular mobility may also pose unique challenges to cells, as complexes with elongated stretches of unstructured regions may prove more prone to extensive aggregation.
evidence: This is speculation about potential negative consequences of prolonged starvation.

claim: Limited diffusion may stimulate aberrant protein aggregation, a process which has been implicated in a wide variety of human diseases.
source: It will now be interesting to explore whether other cell types, including metazoan cells, respond similarly to starvation or growth factor depletion and if limited diffusion indeed stimulates aberrant protein aggregation, a process which has been implicated in a wide variety of human diseases (Ross and Poirier, 2004).
evidence: This is speculation about potential implications for human disease, with a citation to Ross and Poirier, 2004.
